issues: the Mūlagandhakuṭī (精舍) → 精舍, a vihāra (the one just described, housing the stone with the Buddha's footprints); no Mūlagandhakuṭī in the Chinese
en_revised: To the north of the vihāra (精舍) [that houses the stone with the Buddha's footprints] stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, with an inscription recording that King Aśoka thrice offered Jambudvīpa to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thrice redeemed it with precious treasures.

issues: image of the Buddha, which is the shadow left → 留影金佛像, a golden image of (i.e. copying) the shadow left in the cave, not the shadow itself; the mountain is written 前正覺山 here
en_revised: One golden image of the Buddha [modelled on] the shadow left in the Dragon Cave of Mount Prāgbodhi (前正覺山) in the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國), measuring three feet three inches in height including the halo and pedestal.

issues: some being temples (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → 或精舍, vihāras; the gloss is not in the Chinese
en_revised: From here, traveling south for more than a hundred *li*, one arrives at the Bodhi tree (Mahā-bodhi). The wall surrounding the tree is built of brick, high, steep, and extremely solid. It is long from east to west and slightly narrower from north to south. The main gate faces east toward the Nairañjanā River; the south gate connects to a large flower pond; the west side is bordered by steep and solid terrain; and the north gate leads to a large monastery (mahāvihāra). Within it, sacred sites are connected one after another, some being vihāras (精舍) and others being stūpas, all constructed by various kings, ministers, wealthy people, and elders out of admiration for the Holy One, serving as markers.  In the center is the Diamond Throne (vajrāsana). When the Bhadrakalpa was first formed, it arose together with the great earth. It is situated in the center of the trichiliocosm, reaching down to the golden wheel and up to the surface of the ground. It is made of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference. The term "diamond" is used because it is solid and difficult to destroy, capable of crushing all things. If it did not rely on the original foundation, the earth could not remain stable; if one did not use the diamond as a seat, there would be no place capable of sustaining the diamond samādhi. Now, wishing to subdue Māra and attain the Way, one must reside here; if one were on other ground, the earth would tilt and slant, and therefore the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all take their place here. Furthermore, the place of attaining the Way is also called the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); when the world shakes and trembles, this place alone does not move. For one or two hundred years, sentient beings have had little merit, and upon going to the Bodhi tree, they do not see the Diamond Throne. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various kings used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries, seated facing east. It is said that when this Bodhisattva’s body sinks and disappears, the Buddha-dharma will come to an end; currently, the southern Bodhisattva has already sunk up to its chest. The Bodhi tree is the Pippala tree. While the Buddha was alive, it was several hundred feet high, but having been repeatedly cut down by evil kings, it is now over fifty feet tall. Because the Buddha sat beneath it and attained Supreme Enlightenment, it is called the Bodhi tree. The trunk of the tree is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are green and lustrous; they do not wither in autumn or winter. Only on the day of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa do the leaves suddenly fall, only to grow back as they were after a single night. Every year on this day, the kings of various countries and their ministers gather under the tree to wash it with milk, light lamps, scatter flowers, and collect the leaves before departing. When the Master arrived, he paid homage to the Bodhi tree and the image of the Buddha at the time of his enlightenment, which was made by Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩). After gazing at it with utmost sincerity, he prostrated himself on the ground, filled with grief and regret, and lamented to himself: "When the Buddha attained enlightenment, I know not in what realm I was wandering. Now, in this age of the image, I have finally arrived here." Reflecting on how deep and heavy his karmic obstructions were, his eyes filled with tears of sorrow. At that time, the assembly of monks was concluding their summer retreat, and several thousand people from near and far had gathered; there was no one among the observers who did not sob. Within a radius of one yojana of that place, the area is filled with sacred sites; the Master stayed for eight or nine days to complete his circumambulations and acts of homage.

en_revised: To the east of the Bamboo Grove is a stupa built by King Ajātaśatru (阿闍多設咄路王). After the Tathāgata entered nirvana, the various kings divided the relics; King Ajātaśatru, having obtained his portion, brought it back and erected a stupa to make offerings. When King Aśoka resolved to build stupas everywhere, he opened it to take the relics, yet a small portion remained, which now frequently emits a brilliant light.

issues: three knowledges (te-vidyā) → 三明, trividyā; "the fifteenth day of the first summer retreat" → 即初安居十五日時, the fifteenth day after the start of the rains retreat (Beal: the first fifteen days of the Rain-Rest); "due to his power" → 斯其力也 ambiguous: "this is the power of it" (the Buddha's kindness, Beal) or of the compilation; DM kept
en_revised: Traveling five or six li southwest of the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), there is a separate bamboo forest on the side of the mountain, in which there is a large stone chamber (Skt. sapta-parṇa-guhā). This is the place where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa (摩訶迦葉波), together with nine hundred and ninety-nine great Arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. At the time of the compilation, an immeasurable host of holy ones gathered like clouds. Mahākāśyapa announced, "Among the assembly, those who know themselves to possess the three knowledges (trividyā), the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā), and who have mastered the entire Dharma-store of the Tathāgata without error, may remain; the others should each settle where they see fit." At that time, nine hundred and ninety-nine people were selected.  Ānanda was still in the stage of a learner (śaikṣa). Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda, "Your outflows (āsrava) are not yet exhausted; do not defile the pure assembly." Ashamed, Ānanda went out. He practiced diligently for one night, severed the bonds of the three realms, attained the state of an Arhat, and returned to knock at the door. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Are your bonds exhausted?" He replied, "Yes." He further said, "If your bonds are exhausted, there is no need to open the door; enter as you wish." Ānanda then entered through the crack in the door and bowed at the feet of the monks. Mahākāśyapa took his hand and said, "I wanted you to eliminate all outflows and realize the holy fruit, which is why I drove you out. You should know this; do not harbor resentment." Ānanda said, "If I harbored resentment, how could I be called one whose bonds are exhausted?" Thereupon, he offered thanks and sat down. This was on the fifteenth day after the beginning of the summer retreat. Kāśyapa said to Ānanda, "The Tathāgata often praised you among the assembly for your extensive learning and your ability to retain all teachings (dhāraṇī). You may ascend the seat and recite the Sūtrapīṭaka (素呾纜藏), which is the collection of all scriptures, for the assembly." Ānanda accepted the command and rose. He bowed toward the mountain where the Buddha attained parinirvāṇa, then ascended the seat to recite the scriptures, while the assembly recorded them as he spoke. Once the recording was finished, he further commanded Upāli to recite the Vinayapiṭaka (毘柰耶藏), which is the collection of all disciplinary precepts. Once that was recited, Kāśyapa himself recited the Abhidharmapiṭaka (阿毘達磨藏), which is the collection of all treatises. Over the course of the two or three months of the summer retreat, the three piṭakas were collected, written on palm leaves, and then widely circulated. The holy ones said to one another, "Our gathering here is to repay the Buddha’s kindness; that we are able to hear these teachings today is due to his power." Because Mahākāśyapa was the elder (sthavira) among the monks, the group was named the Sthaviravāda (上座部).

issues: the place where Rāhula (度羅怙羅) stayed → 度羅怙羅處, the place where Rāhula was ordained (度 = to ordain, not part of the name) (Beal: where Rahula was received as a disciple)
en_revised: Going three or four li to the northeast, one arrives at the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬多城). The outer wall has already fallen into ruin, but the inner city remains steep and high, measuring over twenty li in circumference, with one gate on each side. When King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) first resided in the Upper Grass Palace, the populace was dense and prosperous, with houses packed together like fish scales. Having suffered several fires, the king established a strict regulation: anyone who was careless and caused a fire to break out first would be banished to the Cold Forest (寒林). The Cold Forest was the place in that country where corpses were abandoned. Before long, the royal palace suddenly caught fire again. The king said, "As I am the lord of the people, if I do not carry out the law upon myself, I have no way to discipline those below." He ordered the Crown Prince to remain and govern, while the king moved to reside in the Cold Forest. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王) heard that Bimbisāra was living outside the city and wished to select troops to attack him. Scouts learned of this and reported it, so the king built a walled town. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was named Rājagṛha (王舍城), which is the New City. Later, King Ajātaśatru (闍王) succeeded to the throne and made it his capital. When King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐), he bestowed this city upon the Brahmins. Today, there are no common people in the city, only about a thousand Brahmin families. In the southwest corner inside the palace city, there is a stūpa; this is the former residence of the elder Jyotiṣka (殊底色迦長者), and nearby is the place where Rāhula (羅怙羅) was ordained (度).

issues: Nālandā Monastery (那爛陀僧伽藍) → the text has 那爛陀寺; "ten billion gold coins" → 十億金錢, ten yi; 億 here is indeterminate (100,000 or 10 million), not a modern billion (Beal: ten lacs); "kanaka flower trees" → 羯尼花樹, karṇikāra (as DM itself has in 09.02.04; Beal: Kie-ni); "divination (śilpasthānavidyā)" → 術數, calculation and divination; śilpasthāna is not meant
en_revised: As for the Nālandā Monastery (那爛陀寺), this is translated as the "Monastery of Bestowing without Weariness." According to the traditions of the elders, to the south of this monastery, in an Āmra (菴沒羅) grove, there is a pond. In the pond lives a dragon named Nālandā; because the monastery was built beside it, it took this as its name. It is also said that when the Tathāgata was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path, he was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for the lonely and the destitute and constantly practiced generous giving; the people remembered his kindness, and thus they named the place "Bestowing without Weariness." The land was originally the garden of the elder Āmra. Five hundred merchants bought it with ten *yi* (十億) of gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and many of the merchants attained the fruits of the path. After the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, a former king of this country, Śakrāditya (鑠迦羅阿迭多), out of reverence and longing for the Buddha, built this monastery. After the king passed away, his son, King Buddhagupta (佛陀毱多王), succeeded to the great heritage and built another monastery to the south. When it came to his son, King Tathāgata (怛他揭多王), he built another monastery to the east. When it came to his son, Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多), he built another monastery to the northeast. Later, seeing a holy monk from this country of China (支那國) traveling to attend to his offerings, he felt joy in his heart and renounced his throne to become a monk. His son, Vajra (伐闍羅), succeeded to the throne and built another monastery to the north. Thereafter, a king of Central India built another monastery to the side. In this way, six emperors in succession each added to the construction, and they further enclosed the exterior with a brick wall, uniting them into a single monastery with one main gate. The courtyards are laid out separately, and the interior is divided into eight halls. Precious terraces are arranged like stars, and jade pavilions stand like mountain peaks; towers rise high into the mist, and halls hover above the rosy clouds, with wind and clouds arising from the doors and windows, and the sun and moon intersecting at the eaves. Moreover, clear waters meander through the grounds where blue lotuses and water lilies bloom, *karṇikāra* (羯尼) flower trees glow brilliantly within, and mango groves grow thick and lush outside. The monks' quarters in all the courtyards are four-story buildings, featuring dragon-carved ridgepoles, rainbow-colored beams, ornate brackets, and vermilion pillars, with carved columns, engraved railings, jade plinths, and decorated rafters; the roof ridges catch the shimmering light, and the eaves are connected by colorful silken cords. The number of monasteries in India is in the tens of thousands, but for magnificence and loftiness, this one is the ultimate. There are always ten thousand monks, both residents and guests, who study the Mahayana as well as the eighteen schools, along with secular classics such as the *Vedas*, and also research logic (*hetuvidyā*), grammar (*śabdavidyā*), medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), and calculation and divination (術數). There are over a thousand people who can explain twenty collections of sutras and commentaries, over five hundred who can explain thirty, and ten people, including the Master, who can explain fifty. Only the Master Śīlabhadra (戒賢) has mastered them all; he is virtuous, eminent, and advanced in years, serving as the master for the entire assembly. Within the monastery, there are over a hundred lecture sessions daily, and the students study and practice without wasting a single moment. The place where such virtuous multitudes reside is naturally solemn. Since its establishment over seven hundred years ago, not a single person has committed a transgression worthy of reproach. The king holds them in high esteem and has granted more than a hundred villages for their sustenance, each consisting of two hundred households, which daily provide several hundred *shi* of polished nonglutinous rice, butter, and milk. Because of this, the students could sit with folded hands and seek nothing, for the four requisites were naturally sufficient; that they achieved success in their arts and studies was due to this power.

issues: (僧娑; the Chinese translation means 'wild goose') → the Life has no such gloss; removed
en_revised: Traveling east for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶山). In front of the monastery on the eastern peak, there is a stūpa called Hamsa (僧娑). Formerly, this monastery followed the gradual teaching of the Hīnayāna and consumed the three kinds of pure meat. On one occasion, when they were unable to purchase or obtain any, the steward was pacing about in distress. He then saw a flock of geese flying by and, looking up, said in jest: "Today the monks' provisions are lacking; the Mahāsattva should know that now is the time." No sooner had he spoken than the leader of the flock responded to his voice, folded its wings in the high clouds, and cast its body down to its death. When the bhikṣus saw this, they were ashamed and fearful. They informed all the monks, and those who heard were shocked and lamented, none failing to weep at the sight. They said to one another: "This is a Bodhisattva. What kind of people are we, that we would dare to eat it? Furthermore, the Tathāgata established his teachings in gradual stages as a safeguard; we have clung to those initial, provisional words as if they were the ultimate doctrine, remaining foolish and unyielding, which has led to this injury. From this day forward, we should follow the Mahāyāna and must no longer eat the three kinds of pure meat." They then built a sacred stūpa and buried the dead goose within it, adding an inscription to commemorate its heart so that its noble deed might be passed down forever; this is the reason for the existence of this stūpa.

issues: the isolated hill of Vyāsa (孤山) → 孤山, simply an isolated hill; "Vyāsa" is invented (Beal: a solitary hill); "central monastery (mūla-gandha-kuṭī)" and "guarding the mūla-gandha-kuṭī" → 精舍, vihāra; "stamped their feet" → 嗚足 may rather be "kissed [his] feet"; DM (and Beal) kept
en_revised: Two or three li to the south of the monastery is an isolated hill (孤山), where the rocky peaks are lofty and precipitous, the shrubs are dense and somber, the springs and ponds are clear and fresh, and the flowers and plants are richly fragrant. As it is a place of excellence, there are many spiritual temples, and the wonders of miraculous transformations and divine anomalies are manifold. In the central vihāra (精舍) there is a sandalwood-carved image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of exceptional spiritual majesty. There are always dozens of people who fast, abstaining from food and drink for seven or fourteen days to pray for their various wishes. Those whose hearts are most sincere will see the Bodhisattva, in all his solemn and majestic splendor with a brilliant light, emerge from the sandalwood image to comfort them and grant their desires. Such miraculous visions occur frequently, and for this reason, the number of those who seek refuge there is ever-increasing. The attendants, fearing that the many visitors might defile the holy image, erected wooden railings about seven paces away on all four sides; thus, those who come to worship must all stay outside the railings and are not permitted to approach the statue. The incense and flowers offered are also scattered from a distance. Those who find the flowers resting on the hands or hanging from the arms of the Bodhisattva consider it an auspicious sign that their wishes will be fulfilled. The Master of the Law wished to go and make a petition, so he bought various flowers and strung them into garlands. Bringing them to the place of the image, he finished offering sincere worship and praise, then knelt before the Bodhisattva and made three vows: "First, if I can return safely to my home country without hindrance after completing my studies here, may the flowers rest upon your hands; second, if the merit and wisdom I have cultivated allow me to be reborn in the Tuṣita (覩史多) Palace to serve Maitreya (慈氏) Bodhisattva as I desire, may the garlands hang upon your arms; third, the holy teachings state that among the realm of sentient beings there are some who lack the Buddha-nature, and I, Xuanzang, am now in doubt as to whether I possess it or not; if I do have the Buddha-nature and can achieve Buddhahood through cultivation, may the garlands hang around your neck." Having finished speaking, he scattered the flowers from a distance, and all landed just as he had requested. Having fulfilled his petitions, he was filled with immeasurable joy. Those nearby who were also worshipping, as well as the people guarding the vihāra (精舍), having seen this, snapped their fingers and stamped their feet, saying, "This has never happened before. When you attain the Way in the future, we pray that you will remember the causal connection of this day and save us first."

issues: The western border of the country is the Gaṅgā River, and to the south it reaches the Small Isolated Hill (Asura-giri) → 國西界殑伽河南至小孤山: on the western border, south of the Gaṅgā, one reaches a small isolated hill (Beal: same); "Asura-giri" not in the Chinese; "five feet two inches long, and four feet one inch wide" is right for the Life (Xiyu ji has 2 ft 1 in wide)
en_revised: From here, traveling gradually, one arrives at the country of Īraṇṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國). There are ten saṃghārāmas with over four thousand monks, who mostly study the Hīnayāna and follow the doctrines of the Sarvāstivāda school. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the country’s ruler and donated the capital city to the monks; within it, two monasteries were built, each housing one thousand monks. There are two monks of great virtue, one named Tathāgatagupta and the other Kṣānti-siṃha, both of whom are well-versed in the Sarvāstivāda school. [Xuanzang] stayed for another year to study the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, and other texts. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Buddha once preached the Dharma to devas and humans for three months; nearby are also the traces of the four past Buddhas. On the western border of the country, south of the Gaṅgā River, one reaches a small isolated hill (小孤山), where the Buddha once spent the three-month summer retreat and subdued the yakṣa Vakula. On a large rock below the mountain’s southeastern cliff is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which is over an inch deep into the stone, five feet two inches long, and four feet one inch wide. There is also a trace of where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (water vessel), which is over an inch deep and shaped like an eight-petaled flower. In the wild forests on the southern border of the country, there are many large elephants, which are robust and tall.

issues: The western border of the country is the Ganges River, and to the south it reaches the Small Isolated Hill (asura) → on the western border, south of the Gaṅgā, one reaches the Small Isolated Hill (Beal: same); "(asura)" not in the Chinese
en_revised: On the western border of the country, south of the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, one reaches the Small Isolated Hill (小孤山), where the Buddha once spent the three-month summer retreat and subdued the yakṣa Vakula (薄句羅). Below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, on a large rock, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which is over an inch deep into the stone, five feet two inches long, and four feet one inch wide. There is also a trace of where the Buddha placed his water vessel (kuṇḍikā), which is over an inch deep and fashioned with an eight-petaled flower pattern.

issues: great mountain forest (pravaragiri) → 大山林; the gloss is not in the Chinese; "On the southern border..., for several tens of yojanas" → 國南界數十由旬 ambiguous: the forest may lie several tens of yojanas toward the southern border; DM kept
en_revised: Following the southern bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā) river, traveling east for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Campā (瞻波國). There are ten monasteries and more than two hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The city walls are made of brick and are several zhang high; the foundation moats are deep and wide, being extremely lofty and secure. In ancient times, at the beginning of the kalpa, people all lived in caves. Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans and went to bathe in the Ganges river; the water spirit touched her body, and she gave birth to four sons. They divided and ruled over Jambudvīpa as kings, demarcating boundaries and building towns and villages; this city is the capital of one of those sons. On the southern border of the country, for several tens of yojanas, there is a great mountain forest, dense and lush, stretching for more than two hundred li. Within it, there are many wild elephants, roaming in herds of several hundred; therefore, the two countries of Iranaparvata (伊爛拏) and Campā have the most elephant troops, and they frequently order elephant trainers to capture and tame them in this forest for national use. Furthermore, it abounds with jackals, rhinoceroses, and black leopards, so that no one dares to travel there. Tradition says that before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was a cowherd tending several hundred cows who drove them into the forest. One cow would leave the herd and go off alone, often disappearing to an unknown place, but when it was time to return at sunset, it would rejoin the herd with a beautiful, radiant luster and an extraordinary lowing that terrified the other cows, none of whom dared to stand before it. After many days of this, the cowherd wondered at the cause and secretly waited to watch it; in a moment the cow left again, and he followed to observe it. He saw the cow enter a hole in the rocks and followed it inside; after about four or five li, it suddenly opened into a bright expanse where the woods and fields were magnificent, filled with many strange flowers and fruits so brilliant they dazzled the eyes, unlike anything seen in the common world. The cow grazed in one place, and the grass was fragrant and lush, also unlike anything in the human realm. The man saw that the fruit trees were yellow and red like gold, fragrant and large, so he plucked one; though he craved it in his heart, he was still afraid and did not dare to eat it. After a while the cow came out and the man followed it to return, but when he reached the aperture in the rocks and had not yet emerged, an evil demon snatched the fruit and kept it. The cowherd asked a great physician about this and described the appearance of the fruit; the physician said that it should not be eaten immediately, but that he should find a way to bring one out. The next day he again followed the cow inside and picked another fruit, intending to bring it back in his bosom, but the demon again blocked him to snatch it; the man put the fruit into his mouth, and when the demon gripped his throat, the man swallowed it. Once the fruit entered his stomach, his body became enormous; although his head could get out, his body remained stuck in the hole, and he could not return. Later, his family members searched for him and, seeing his transformed state, were all terrified, yet he was still able to speak and explain what had happened. His family returned and summoned many laborers to try to pull him out, but he could not be moved. The king heard of this and came to observe it himself; fearing it might become a future calamity, he sent men to dig and pull, but he still could not be moved. As months and years passed, he gradually turned into stone, though he still retained the shape of a person. Later, another king, knowing that it had been transformed by a divine fruit (仙菓), said to his attendants: "Since his body was transformed because of the medicine, his body itself is the medicine; although it appears to be stone, its substance is ultimately divine, so we should send someone to take a small piece with a hammer and chisel." The ministers followed the king's command and went with craftsmen to chisel it with all their might, but after ten days, they could not obtain a single piece; it still exists today.

en_revised: From here, he crossed the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east and traveled more than six hundred li to reach the country of Puṇḍravardhana (奔那伐彈那國). He sought out and paid homage to the sacred sites; there were more than twenty monasteries and over three thousand monks, who studied both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. More than twenty li to the west of the city was the Vāśibha (跋姞婆) Monastery, with its lofty and magnificent terraces and pavilions, housing seven hundred monks. Beside it was a stūpa built by King Aśoka at the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months, which frequently emitted light. There were also the traces of the walking meditation of the four Buddhas. Nearby was a vihāra (精舍), in which there was an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; if one prayed with utmost sincerity, there was no wish that would not be fulfilled.

More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vāśibha Monastery (跋姞婆伽藍), with its lofty and magnificent terraces and pavilions, housing seven hundred monks. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the site where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma for three months; it frequently emits brilliant light. There are also the traces of the walking paths of the four Buddhas. Nearby is a vihāra (精舍), containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); those who pray with utmost sincerity never fail to have their wishes fulfilled.

en_revised: Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttikā Monastery (絡多末知僧伽藍). In former times, before the Buddhadharma had reached this country, a śramaṇa from South India traveled to this land and defeated the heterodox doctrines of a heretic who wore a metal plate over his belly; the king of the country then established it for him.

en_revised: From here, passing south into a great forest and traveling southeast for more than nine hundred li, one arrives at the country of Andhra (案達羅國). Beside the city is a large monastery, with magnificent and imposing carvings and structures, and statues that are beautiful and solemn. In front of it is a stone stupa, several hundred feet high, built by the Arhat Ācāra.

issues: the solitary hill of Vyāsa (孤山) → 孤山, a solitary hill; "Vyāsa" is invented
en_revised: More than twenty li to the southwest of the Arhat monastery is a solitary hill (孤山), upon which there is a stone stūpa; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dignāga composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic).

issues: From the borders of this country, it is over three thousand li to the country of Malakuṭa → 自此國界三千餘里，聞有秣羅矩吒國: he heard that there is Malakuṭa over 3000 li from the borders; the hearsay 聞 is dropped, making it read as a visit (Beal: It is reported that ...)
en_revised: He heard that over three thousand *li* from the borders of this country there is the country of Malakuṭa (秣羅矩吒國); situated by the sea, it is extremely abundant in exotic treasures. To the east of its capital city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, where in the past the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and manifested great divine transformations, a place where he delivered immeasurable multitudes. To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with its lofty cliffs and deep valleys. Within it are white sandalwood trees and *candaneva* trees; the latter resemble poplars and are cool in nature, so many serpents cling to them, only hibernating in winter, which is how they are distinguished from other sandalwood. There are also *karpūra* (羯布羅) fragrance trees, with trunks like pines but different leaves, and their flowers and fruits are also distinct. When moist, they have no scent, but after being harvested and dried, a fragrance is found within when broken, shaped like mica and colored like ice and snow; this is what is called Borneo camphor (龍腦香).

en_revised: He also heard that there is a city by the sea in the northeast, from which one travels more than three thousand li to the southeast to reach the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國).
